name: Mumbai
info: Mumbai, also called Bombay, is a port city on the Konkan coast of western India, built on an archipelago of seven islands, ruled in turn by Indian dynasties, sultanates, the Portuguese and the British, and now the capital of Maharashtra.

facts.founded: People lived on the islands from the Stone Age, and the islands became part of the Maurya Empire under Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE; the Koli fishing community had long inhabited them.
facts.where: On the Konkan coast of western India, on what was originally an archipelago of seven islands with a deep natural harbour on the Arabian Sea, in the state of Maharashtra.
facts.known: A harbour of the Konkan coast; the Kanheri Caves and Elephanta Caves; Portuguese and then British Bombay; the Hornby Vellard; India's first passenger railway; cotton mills and trade; the Indian National Congress and the independence movement; Bollywood
facts.today: Mumbai is the capital of the Indian state of Maharashtra and a city of more than 12 million people.

t: The seven islands passed from Koli fishing settlements to the Mauryas and later Indian dynasties, to the Delhi and Gujarat sultanates, to the Portuguese in 1535 and to the English Crown in 1661, which leased them to the East India Company in 1668.

The Company made Bombay a port and its main base on the west coast, and the Hornby Vellard of 1784, the railway of 1853 and the cotton boom of the 1860s turned the islands into one large trading city.

Bombay hosted the first session of the Indian National Congress in 1885, became the capital of Maharashtra in 1960 and took the name Mumbai in the 1990s, after riots and bombings that killed many of its people.
dyk: The seven islands of Bombay were joined into a single landmass by the Hornby Vellard, an engineering project begun in 1782 that was first rejected by the East India Company in 1783 and was completed in 1784.
ev: The islands become part of the Maurya Empire under Ashoka
The Silhara dynasty of Konkan begins to rule the region, holding it until 1260
The islands are ceded to the Portuguese under the Treaty of Bassein
Bombay passes to the English Crown as part of Catherine of Braganza’s dowry
The Crown leases the islands to the East India Company for £10 a year
The Hornby Vellard is completed and joins the seven islands
India’s first passenger railway opens between Bombay and Thane
Bombay becomes the capital of the new state of Maharashtra

sections.origins:
Mumbai stands on the Konkan coast of western India, where a deep natural harbour opens on the Arabian Sea. The city was built on what was originally an archipelago of seven islands: the Isle of Bombay, Parel, Mazagaon, Mahim, Colaba, Worli and Old Woman’s Island, also called Little Colaba. Pleistocene sediments found near Kandivali in northern Mumbai by the British archaeologist Malcolm Todd in 1939 indicate habitation since the Stone Age, and the Koli fishing community had long lived on the islands. The Koli goddess Mumbadevi, called Mumbā or Mahā-Ambā, is believed to have given the city its name, with ā’ī meaning “mother” in Marathi.

In the 3rd century BCE the islands became part of the Maurya Empire under Ashoka, and the Satavahanas held them from the 2nd century BCE. The Kanheri Caves became an important centre of Buddhism in western India. The port of Sopara, in present-day Nala Sopara, was an important trading centre in the 1st century BCE, with trade contacts with Rome. In the 2nd century the Greek geographer Ptolemy called the islands Heptanesia, “a cluster of seven islands”. The Portuguese writer Gaspar Correia recorded the name Bombaim after 1512, and in 1516 Duarte Barbosa used Tana-Maiambu. The derivation of Bombay from a supposed Portuguese phrase for “good little bay” has no scientific basis.
sections.growth:
Under the Portuguese the main trade of the islands was coconuts and coir. The city’s growth began under the English East India Company, which built a quay, warehouses and a customs house after 1668. Governor Gerald Aungier established the first mint in 1670 and offered business incentives that attracted Parsis, Goans, Jews, Dawoodi Bohras, Gujarati Banias and Brahmins. The population rose from about 10,000 in 1661 to 60,000 by 1675. In the late 1680s the Company moved its main holdings from Surat to Bombay. By the end of the 17th century the port traded in salt, rice, ivory, cloth, lead and sword blades with many Indian ports and with Mecca and Basra. Shipbuilding began in 1735, and in 1750 Lovji Nusserwanjee Wadia built the Bombay Dock, the first dry dock commissioned in Asia.

The Hornby Vellard, begun in 1782 and completed in 1784, united the seven islands, and reclamation at Worli and Mahalaxmi followed. India’s first passenger railway ran between Bombay and Thane from 16 April 1853, the first cotton mill opened at Tardeo in 1854, and the University of Bombay was founded in 1857. The American Civil War cut cotton supplies from the United States and brought a boom in the cotton trade, and the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 changed the port’s sea trade. The Bombay Stock Exchange was established in 1875. Until the 1970s the city’s prosperity rested largely on its textile mills and seaport; the Jawaharlal Nehru Port was commissioned at Nhava Sheva in 1989.
sections.rulers:
After the Mauryas and Satavahanas the islands were ruled by a succession of dynasties, among them the Western Satraps, Abhiras, Vakatakas, Kalachuris, Konkan Mauryas, Chalukyas and Rashtrakutas. The Shilaharas of Konkan ruled the region from 810 to 1260. In the late 13th century King Bhima, called Bhimdev in one account, set up a kingdom with its capital at Mahikawati, present-day Mahim, and around 1298 the Pathare Prabhus came to Mahim from Saurashtra in Gujarat. The Delhi Sultanate took the islands in the late 1340s, and they were then governed by the Gujarat Sultanate. The Gujarat and Bahmani sultanates contested them between 1429 and 1431.

Sultan Bahadur Shah of Gujarat, apprehensive of the Mughal emperor Humayun, signed the Treaty of Bassein with the Portuguese on 23 December 1534, and the islands were ceded to them on 25 October 1535. In 1661 the islands passed to the English as part of Catherine of Braganza’s dowry on her marriage to Charles II, and under the Royal Charter of 27 March 1668 the Crown leased them to the East India Company for an annual rent of £10. The Marathas under Peshwa Baji Rao I captured Salsette in 1737 and Bassein in 1739, and Salsette passed to the British in 1774, confirmed by the Treaty of Salbai in 1782. After the Company defeated the last Peshwa, Baji Rao II, in 1817, Bombay was the capital of the Bombay Presidency under British rule. After independence in 1947 it became the capital of Bombay State, and from 1 May 1960 of Maharashtra.
sections.life:
The city drew many peoples. The Koli were its old fishing community, and the Pathare Prabhus were among its earliest settlers. Under the Portuguese the Roman Catholic orders, particularly the Franciscans and Jesuits, built churches, and the East Indian Catholics were converted by the Portuguese in the 16th century. Dorabji Nanabhoy was the first Parsi to settle in Bombay, in 1640. Jews settled in the 18th century, among them the Bene Israeli from the Konkan villages. In the mid-18th century migrants arrived from many parts of the subcontinent and from Madagascar. Marathi is the most spoken language, followed by Hindi, Urdu and Gujarati, and a colloquial Bombay Hindi is spoken in the streets.

Bombay was an early centre of printing and the press: Bhimjee Parikh imported the first printing press in 1670, the Bombay Herald appeared in 1789 and the Bombay Courier in 1790, and the Gujarati newspaper Bombay Samachar has been published since 1822. Elphinstone High School opened in 1822, Wilson College in 1832 and the Grant Medical College in 1845. After the fire of 17 February 1803 destroyed many localities around the Old Fort, the British planned a new town with wider roads. Mumbai is also described as the birthplace of Indian cinema, and the Hindi film industry based there is called Bollywood, a blend of Bombay and Hollywood. Dharavi, in central Mumbai, houses about a million people.
sections.crises:
The islands were attacked often in the 17th century. Yakut Khan, an admiral of the Mughal Empire, landed in October 1672 and ravaged the inhabitants. The Dutch governor-general Rickloffe van Goen attacked on 20 February 1673, and Aungier resisted him. Yakut Khan landed again in 1689, razed Mazagon Fort in June 1690 and left on 8 June 1690 after the British paid Aurangzeb. A fire on 17 February 1803 razed many localities, and a severe famine in May 1804 led to large-scale emigration. Riots broke out between Muslims and Parsis in 1851 and again in 1874, and on 11 August 1893 a riot between Hindus and Muslims, after a Shiva temple was attacked, killed 75 people and injured 350.

From September 1896 a bubonic plague epidemic struck; the death toll was estimated at 1,900 people a week, and about 850,000 people, half the population, fled. A riot against the plague measures began on 9 March 1898 and led to a strike of dock and railway workers. The Great Bombay Textile Strike began on 18 January 1982, with nearly 250,000 workers in more than 50 mills. Riots in May 1984 killed 278 people and wounded 1,118. After the demolition of the Babri Mosque at Ayodhya, communal riots between Hindus and Muslims in December 1992 and January 1993 killed more than 1,000 people. On 12 March 1993 thirteen coordinated bombs killed 257 people and injured more than 700. Bombs on suburban trains on 11 July 2006 killed 209 and injured over 700. Ten armed men attacked the city from 26 to 29 November 2008, and 164 people died and 308 were injured. Three blasts on 13 July 2011 killed 26.
sections.legacy:
Bombay was a base of the Indian independence movement. The first session of the Indian National Congress met there from 28 to 31 December 1885, the Rowlatt Satyagraha of 1919 had its main centre in the city, the Quit India movement was proclaimed there on 7 August 1942, and the Royal Indian Navy Mutiny began on 18 February 1946. The last British troops to leave India, the First Battalion of the Somerset Light Infantry, passed through the arcade of the Gateway of India on 28 February 1948, ending the 282 years of British presence in Bombay. In 1960, after protests by the Samyukta Maharashtra movement in which 105 people were killed by police firing, the Flora Fountain was renamed Hutatma Chowk, “Martyr’s Square”, in their memory.

The city’s buildings are mostly Gothic Revival, Indo-Saracenic and Art Deco in style. The Victoria Terminus, completed in 1888, was renamed Chhatrapati Shivaji Terminus in 1996, and the Elephanta Caves, the terminus and the Victorian and Art Deco Ensemble are World Heritage Sites. Marathi nationalists, led by the Shiv Sena, insisted on the change of the name Bombay to Mumbai in the 1990s, arguing that Bombay echoed colonial rule; some residents still use the old name. Mumbai is the capital of Maharashtra, and more than 12 million people live in the city proper.

summary: Mumbai grew from an archipelago of seven islands on the Konkan coast, held by Indian dynasties, sultanates, the Portuguese and from 1661 the English. The East India Company made it a port and cotton city, and it was a base of the independence movement. It is the capital of Maharashtra.
references: M. D. David, History of Bombay, 1661–1708 (University of Mumbai, 1973)
M. D. David, Bombay, the city of dreams: a history of the first city in India (Himalaya Publishing House, 1995)
Sharada Dwivedi, Bombay: The Cities Within (Eminence Designs, 2001)
Amar Farooqui, Opium city: the making of early Victorian Bombay (Three Essays Press, 2006)
Thomas Blom Hansen, Wages of violence: naming and identity in postcolonial Bombay (Princeton University Press, 2001)
notes: START: neither article gives a founding date. I used -250 (circa), the 3rd century BCE when the islands joined the Maurya Empire; people lived there from the Stone Age.

DISAGREEMENTS left out or made vague: (1) Delhi Sultanate conquest 1348 (History) vs 1347-48 (main): written 'late 1340s'. (2) Gujarat Sultanate start 1391 (History) vs 1407 (main): dates left out. (3) Plague of 1896: History gives 1,900 deaths per week and 850,000 fled; main gives more than 20,000 killed. I used only the History's weekly estimate; the 20,000 figure left out as not clearly comparable. (4) 2008 attacks: 164 deaths (History) vs 173 (main): written 'more than 160'. (5) Yakut Khan: 'Siddi admiral' (History) vs 'Koli admiral' (main): written 'an admiral of the Mughal Empire'. (6) Company headquarters moved to Bombay 1686 (History) vs 1687 (main): 'late 1680s'. (7) Cession of the islands: main says 11 May 1661 for the dowry, History says marriage treaty 8 May 1661: written '1661'. (8) Kanheri Caves: mid 3rd century BCE (History) vs 1st century CE (main): date left out. (9) Haji Ali Dargah at Mahim (History) vs Worli (main), St Michael's Church 1540 vs 1534, St Andrew's 1575 vs 1580: all left out. (10) Hornby Vellard: History says finished 1784; main says the reclamation project was completed in 1845 and also 'completed by 1784': I used 1784. (11) Bombay Municipal Corporation 1872 (History) vs 1888 (main): left out. (12) Renaming: November 1995 (main) vs 6 March 1996 (History): written 'in the 1990s'. (13) 2005 floods: 83 deaths (History) vs 500-1000 (main): deaths left out. (14) Koli described as Dravidian in origin (History) vs Marathi-speaking (main): left out.

The riots of 1992-93 are told with the figure both articles give (more than 1,000). The 1993 bombings' attribution differs (History: believed orchestrated by Dawood Ibrahim in retaliation; main: Islamic extremists and the Mumbai underworld): left out. The 2008 attackers are described only as ten armed men (History says Pakistani); nationality left out to avoid a verdict.

The 1984 riot (278 killed, 1,118 wounded) is dated 17 May 1984 in History; I wrote 'May 1984' and omitted the trigger. The 1893 riot is attributed in History to an attack on a Shiva temple by Muslims; I wrote only that the temple was attacked.

Bombay Samachar 'has been published since 1822' is the main article's wording. 'Birthplace of Indian cinema' is attributed with 'is also described as'. 'Dharavi houses about a million people' is the articles' present-tense figure.

The 'Bombay Presidency in 1662' remark in the main article (the capital of the Presidency 'in 1662') is out of line with the rest and left out. 'The 282-year-long period of the British in Bombay' is from History.
